paras: The lynching of Cherry Nichols was the killing of a Black youth of about 17 or 18 who was taken from the Bienville Parish jail at Sparta, Louisiana, on a Saturday night in May 1881 by a party of forty to fifty armed men and later found hanged and shot. Nichols was being held for the grand jury, accused of raping and killing a young Black girl. Wire reports carried the story nationally, noting that the men were "mostly colored."

According to a Shreveport Standard account reprinted in the Louisiana Capitolian, the girl's parents left her and an older boy at home with their baby while they went to church on a Sunday, and on returning found both children gone. Her feet were found on the Tuesday sticking out of a sink about eighty yards from the cabin, and the paper reported that she had been raped and beaten with a pine knot.

The boy was caught that evening by two white men and chained in a cotton-house, but by morning he was gone. A cattle buyer, James Riley, told the Standard that on the Wednesday he met "full five hundred people, white and black," many armed, hunting the boy on the Mount Lebanon road. The Claiborne Guardian of Homer reported that Deputy Sheriff I. N. Glover arrested Cherry Nichols within the town of Homer and took him to the jail at Sparta to await the grand jury; the Morehouse Clarion likewise said he had fled to Homer and was held at Sparta for trial.

According to the Sparta Rural Times, at about 11 o'clock on Saturday night, six men woke Sheriff Whitlow, said they were newcomers from the lower part of the parish, and asked him to jail a "hog thief" they called Dock. When the sheriff unlocked the jail, a larger party of white and colored men who had hidden in a clump of woods surrounded the doors and demanded Cherry Nichols. The Rural Times said the men were "remonstrated with" for perhaps half an hour and that the sheriff, facing forty or fifty armed men with the prison open, surrendered the prisoner. Nichols was marched off toward Mount Lebanon and was found on Monday in an old field about six miles north of Sparta, hanging from a tree and "literally shot to pieces."

On the day the body was found, the parish coroner, Dr. Harrell, summoned a jury and held a post-mortem examination at the scene; the surviving text breaks off before any verdict, and no report of arrests or a trial was found.

The first report came from a New Orleans Democrat special from Homer, which the Memphis Appeal printed on May 10 under the headline "Deserved His Doom" and the Wheeling Intelligencer under "Another Brutal Negro Lynched." The wire stated as fact that the boy had "admitted" the crime, and the Washington Evening Star's condensed version said he "confessed"; neither the Homer nor the Sparta papers reported a confession. Within a week the dispatch ran from Richmond to Sacramento, sometimes garbled, as in the Silver State's "Beanfield parish jail at Spark."

The Louisiana papers treated the accusation as established; the Morehouse Clarion called it a "fiendish crime," and the Shreveport Standard called a tree "the best place" for the boy's body. The Sparta Rural Times described the party in a light tone, calling it "a perfect little army" and joking that the decoy prisoner "wouldn't walk worth a cent," while defending the sheriff's surrender as the only sensible course. A New Orleans special of May 23, headed "A Ravisher Lynched" in the Chicago Tribune, first named Nicholls on the wire, and news summaries repeated it.

Most versions say Saturday night, matching the Rural Times' 11 o'clock, but the Wheeling Intelligencer printed "Saturday afternoon." The late Chicago Tribune dispatch of May 23 said the lynching happened "on Saturday," which would point to May 21, but the Homer paper had already reported the hanging on May 11, so the earlier Saturday is better supported. The girl's age is eight in the wire but six in two Louisiana papers, and the party is "mostly colored" in the wire but "both white and colored" in the Rural Times.
